A payment service wants to anticipate another payment to a merchant while
continuing to prioritize disputes. This example adds payment channel and
account tenure, then asks whether shared context is useful for both outcomes.

::: {.callout-note title="Fictional benchmark"}
All data, schemas, and results on this page are fictional placeholders.
No benchmark has been run.
:::

## Example

One fictional labeled observation follows the recurring-merchant example from
[Learning From Event Histories](../guides/learning-from-event-data.qmd):

```yaml
account_age_days: 420
trxns:
  - booked_at: "2026-03-28T09:00:00"
    amount: 24.00
    merchant: Harbor Internet
    channel: direct_debit
    disputed: false
    repeats_next_30_days: true
  - booked_at: "2026-04-28T09:00:00"
    amount: 24.00
    merchant: Harbor Internet
    channel: direct_debit
    disputed: false
    repeats_next_30_days: true
  - booked_at: "2026-05-27T08:00:00"
    amount: 32.00
    merchant: Station Cafe
    channel: card
    disputed: true
    repeats_next_30_days: false
  - booked_at: "2026-05-28T09:00:00"
    amount: 24.00
    merchant: Harbor Internet
    channel: direct_debit
    disputed: false
    repeats_next_30_days: true
```

The common cutoff is May 28, 2026 at 09:00. For every transaction,
`repeats_next_30_days` means another payment to its merchant during the following
30 days; `disputed` means a new dispute against that transaction during the
same window. Both answers are attached only after the window is complete.
Harbor Internet's repeated appearances share the same future merchant-repeat
answer at this cutoff. The target does not identify subscriptions or assume
that a calendar month always lasts 30 days.

<details class="proof-details">
<summary>Complete model schema</summary>

```python
import relflow as rf

model = rf.Model.xs(
    account_age_days=rf.Number,
    trxns=rf.Branch(
        length=32,
        overflow="tail",
        booked_at=rf.DateParts(
            dateparts=["day_of_month", "day_of_week", "hour_of_day"],
        ),
        amount=rf.Number,
        merchant=rf.Category,
        channel=rf.Enum(values=("card", "direct_debit", "bank_transfer")),
        disputed=rf.Boolean(mask=True),
        repeats_next_30_days=rf.Boolean(mask=True),
    ),
)
```

The anonymous root contains the profile and transaction collection. Histories
are oldest to newest, and the last 32 are retained. Account age and channel must
be known at the cutoff. `DateParts` encodes the chosen calendar cycles, not
elapsed-time gaps. This fictional schema uses the calendar-only timing inputs
from the event-history guide; it is a separate comparison from B001's duration
example.

Prediction records omit both outcome fields from every transaction. Both
results appear under `predictions.trxns[i]`, with `inferred: true` at every
retained position.

</details>

## Comparison

Compare separate gradient-boosted tree models with the joint sequence model
above. The trees receive the same profile and transaction attributes, plus
spending, merchant-frequency, and channel summaries over the same history.
Neither model receives either future label as input.

Evaluate repeat ranking and probability quality separately from dispute
ranking. Also compare the joint sequence model with one sequence model per
task before attributing value to shared training.

## Result

| Fictional model | Repeat PR-AUC ↑ | Repeat Brier score ↓ | Dispute PR-AUC ↑ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Separate trees with history summaries | 0.76 | 0.108 | 0.31 |
| Joint RelFlow transaction sequence | 0.78 | 0.115 | 0.33 |

: Fictional placeholder results for the proposed comparison. {#tbl-benchmark-repeat-payments}

The example shows a mixed result: the sequence model ranks better, while the
tree baseline has the lower repeat Brier score. Report ranking and probability
quality separately so the team can assess both outcomes.

<details class="proof-details">
<summary>Fictional method, splits, and controls</summary>

### Cohort and outcome

The imaginary cohort contains accounts with card, direct-debit, or bank-transfer
payments and one review snapshot per account. Every listed transaction has
settled Boolean labels for both next-30-day outcomes. Profile values, merchant
normalization, and event attributes use only information available at the
snapshot cutoff.

Repeat labels refer to the merchant, not an exact amount, payment channel, or
subscription contract. A transaction disputed after the cutoff need not be
fraud. Missing or incomplete outcome windows are not negative labels.

### Proposed split

| Split | Fictional snapshot cutoffs |
| --- | --- |
| Train | January–August 2025 |
| Validation | October–November 2025 |
| Test | January–June 2026 |

Accounts are disjoint across splits, with intervening months separating label
windows. Learn vocabularies and preprocessing state on training only. Use
validation for model choices and any probability calibration, then preserve
those choices for test.

These imaginary paths describe prepared application inputs; no files or
trained artifacts accompany this page:

```python
data = rf.ArrowDataModule(
    model=model,
    train="fictional/repeat-payments/train.parquet",
    validate="fictional/repeat-payments/validation.parquet",
    test="fictional/repeat-payments/test.parquet",
)
```

### Controls for a real run

- Keep accounts, retained histories, label windows, and tuning budgets matched
  across models. Add channel and profile context in separate ablations.
- Supervise both targets on every transaction. For repeat evaluation, average
  scores within each account–merchant–cutoff group and count that group once;
  repeated Harbor Internet records must not inflate its evaluation weight.
- Calculate repeat PR-AUC as average precision and Brier score on those grouped
  probabilities. Calculate dispute PR-AUC per retained transaction.
- Compare joint and separate sequence models using identical inputs. Separate
  task models exclude the other outcome field entirely.
- Repeat training seeds and estimate uncertainty by resampling accounts. Report
  both tasks, including regressions, before choosing a model for an application.

</details>
